What is different about planning an event in New South Wales?

New South Wales holds the largest concentration of working event planners in the country, and the most consistent habit of holding the event somewhere other than where you live. A Sydney couple booking the Hunter Valley, the Southern Highlands, the Blue Mountains or the South Coast is completely ordinary, which means a large share of planners here are used to running an event two hours from their own kitchen table.

Search behaviour follows that split too. People look for event planners NSW wide when they have not settled on a venue, and for a council or a district once they have. Both journeys end in the same place, which is a planner who has worked where your event is.

It also means Greater Sydney is not one market. The Northern Beaches has no railway. Western Sydney runs several degrees hotter in summer and hosts guest lists two or three times the national average. The Hills has acreage where a marquee is a normal answer. Those differences are why nineteen councils, districts and regional markets carry their own page here rather than a single Sydney page pretending to speak for all of them.

On the ground

What planning in New South Wales actually involves

01

Peak season runs October to April

Sydney and the coast fill first for spring and autumn. A Saturday in March or October is the hardest date in the state to book late, and a planner engaged inside six months will be working with whatever is left rather than a shortlist.

02

Public land needs a permit

Harbour foreshore, headland reserves, beaches and most parks sit on council or National Parks land. A permit takes weeks, caps numbers, and almost never gives you exclusive use, so your guests share the view with the public.

03

Distance is measured in time, not kilometres

A 40 kilometre trip across Sydney on a Saturday afternoon can take 90 minutes. Planners here build run sheets around traffic and transfers rather than distance, and they are usually right to.

Timing

When to start planning in New South Wales

Sydney and the coast fill from the outside in: the venue goes first, then the planner, then everyone else. These are the windows people in this state actually work to.

Typical booking windows reported by Australian planners for a Saturday event.
What you are bookingWhen people here usually startWhy that window

If your date is already inside these windows

Start with on-the-day coordination rather than assuming full planning is off the table. A coordinator engaged late still removes the worst of the last month, and several planners will quote a compressed partial plan if you ask for one specifically.

Questions

Planning an event in New South Wales

How much does an event planner cost in New South Wales?

Rates track the market rather than the state. Easy Weddings, in a guide updated in February 2026, puts day-of coordination at roughly $1,500 to $2,000 and full-service planning at $5,000 to $6,000 nationally, and Sydney sits at or above the top of both. Western Sydney and the Hunter generally quote lower, and a regional event adds travel and often a night of accommodation.

Do Sydney planners work in the Hunter Valley and the Southern Highlands?

Routinely, and many of them prefer it. Both regions are inside a two hour drive of Sydney and a large share of the weddings held there are booked by Sydney couples. Expect a travel fee and, for a Saturday, one night of accommodation for the planner. Ask how many site visits are included before the week of the event, because that is where the cost sits.

Which Greater Sydney area should I choose?

Choose the one your venue is in, not the one you live in. The pages are organised by where the event happens, because that is what determines the travel, the parking, the permits and the supplier list. If your ceremony and reception sit in different council areas, use the reception, since that is where the long half of the day happens.

Is a NSW planner different to a Sydney planner?

In practice the state market is the Sydney market plus Newcastle, Wollongong and a set of destination regions. There is no separate body of NSW planners. What changes outside the city is depth: in a regional town you may have three planners to choose from rather than thirty, so starting earlier matters more than it does in Sydney.
